opus-5.5.text:
What excites me most is less any single molecule and more the way the work got done. With the Virtual Lab, we set up a team of AI agents that mirrors how a real interdisciplinary research group operates. There's a principal investigator agent that sets the agenda and keeps the discussion on track, a few scientist agents with different areas of expertise, and a critic agent whose whole job is to poke holes in the reasoning. They hold team meetings, break into individual working sessions, debate tradeoffs, and converge on a plan. A human researcher stays in the loop, giving high-level guidance, but most of the scientific discussion happens among the agents.

What surprised me was how much of the creative, strategic thinking the agents could take on. They weren't just running a tool we handed them. They talked through which overall approach made sense, which existing computational tools were worth combining, and how to structure the workflow. Then they actually wrote the code to stitch it together. That's a different kind of contribution from what we've usually seen from AI in science, where it's mostly a very good tool inside a human-designed pipeline.

The other piece I find meaningful is that we didn't stop at in silico results. We took the agents' proposals into a wet lab and tested them experimentally. A good fraction of the designs behaved well, and some showed promising properties. To me, that closing of the loop, from AI-driven ideation to real-world validation, is what makes this more than a demo.

More broadly, I think it points toward a future where a small human team can work with a group of AI collaborators that brings a lot of different expertise to a problem. That could really accelerate the pace of discovery, especially for labs that don't have every specialist under one roof. It also raises important questions about oversight and about making sure humans stay meaningfully engaged in steering the science, which I think is the right place for people to stay.

fable-5.1.text:
What excites me most is that this was one of the first times we saw a team of AI agents carry out genuinely interdisciplinary science from start to finish, and have it end in a real experimental result.

We built something we call the Virtual Lab, where an AI principal investigator convenes a team of specialist agents, each playing a different scientific role, along with a critic whose job is to challenge the group's assumptions. They hold meetings, argue through the tradeoffs, and converge on a research plan together. What struck me was how much of the reasoning was genuinely theirs. They made sensible judgment calls about strategy, chose how to combine the available computational tools, and wrote the pipeline to connect them.

The piece that really matters to me is that the work didn't stop at a nice-looking proposal on a screen. The candidates the agents suggested were handed off to human scientists in the wet lab and actually tested at the bench. Some of them held up experimentally. To me that closes a loop that's usually missing in AI-for-science demos, where everything stays in silico.

So the thing I keep coming back to is less any single molecule and more the workflow itself. It's a glimpse of how human researchers and teams of agents might collaborate, where the agents handle a lot of the tedious integration and bookkeeping, surface ideas a single person might not, and let the human scientists focus on judgment, oversight, and the experiments that ground everything in reality.

astra-6.text:
What’s exciting to me is that this gives us a way to connect AI reasoning to experimental science. The agents aren’t just discussing a scientific problem—they have to turn that discussion into concrete nanobody designs that you can make and test in the lab.

And nanobody design brings together different kinds of expertise. You need to think about the biology of the target, the structure of the interaction, and the computational tools you can use to propose and evaluate candidates. The Virtual Lab lets agents take on those different perspectives and critique one another’s proposals.

But the key is closing the loop with experiments. A design can look very compelling computationally and still fail in practice. So the exciting question is whether that collaboration produces useful molecules—and whether the experimental feedback can help guide the next round of designs.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s exciting to me is that the agents can go beyond discussing scientific ideas and actually propose designs that we can test experimentally. With the Virtual Lab, we brought together AI agents with different scientific specialties, and they worked through the problem of designing new nanobodies together—suggesting approaches, critiquing one another, and refining a research plan.

Nanobodies are a particularly interesting test case because you have to connect computational predictions to real biological function. A design can look promising on a computer and still fail in the lab. So the exciting part is closing that loop: can a collaboration among AI agents produce something that a scientist can make and measure? That’s a much more meaningful standard for scientific usefulness than whether an agent gives a convincing answer.
